investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: What is the single main determinant of blood culture yield?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Adequate blood volume — around 8–10 mL per adult bottle. Under-filling is a leading cause of false-negative cultures.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: How do you distinguish a coagulase-negative staph contaminant from a true pathogen?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Contaminant is likely if only 1 of 2 sets is positive with a long time-to-positivity. A true pathogen is likely if BOTH sets grow the SAME organism with a short time-to-positivity.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Which organisms are almost never contaminants when grown from blood?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Staph aureus, Strep pneumoniae, E. coli/Enterobacterales, and Candida — treat as real in any set until proven otherwise.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: What workup does Staph aureus bacteraemia (SAB) mandate?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Search for endocarditis/deep focus (echocardiography), remove any lines, and take repeat cultures to confirm clearance.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Regarding timing, how do blood cultures relate to antibiotics in sepsis?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Take cultures BEFORE antibiotics (part of Sepsis 6), but never delay antibiotics in septic shock beyond the recommended window to obtain them.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: What counts as "significant bacteriuria" on urine culture, and what is the commonest causative organism?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Classically ≥10^5 CFU/mL of a single organism (lower counts can be significant with symptoms or pyuria). Commonest organism = E. coli.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Define sterile pyuria and give its key causes.
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Raised urinary WBCs (pyuria) with a negative routine culture. Causes: renal TB (send early-morning urines for AFB), chlamydia/urethritis, recent/partially treated UTI, renal stones, interstitial nephritis, and indwelling catheter.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: When should asymptomatic bacteriuria be treated?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Generally NOT treated. Exceptions: pregnancy (reduces pyelonephritis/preterm birth risk) and before urological instrumentation/TURP. Avoid treating colonisation in elderly/catheterised patients.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Which urinary organism is associated with alkaline urine and struvite (staghorn) stones, and why?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Proteus — it is urease-producing, splitting urea to ammonia which raises urinary pH and promotes struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stone formation.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: What does a high squamous epithelial cell count on urine microscopy indicate?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Skin/genital contamination of the specimen — the sample was not a good clean-catch midstream urine; repeat with a properly collected MSU.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: On a sputum Gram film, what distinguishes a good lower-respiratory sample from salivary contamination?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Good sample = many neutrophils + few squamous epithelial cells. Poor/salivary sample = many epithelial cells + few neutrophils (upper-airway contamination), which should be rejected or interpreted with caution.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Which respiratory pathogens will NOT grow on routine sputum culture, and how are they detected?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Atypicals — Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila and Chlamydophila. Detect via urinary antigen (Legionella, pneumococcus), serology or PCR. Mycobacterium tuberculosis also needs specific AFB smear + mycobacterial culture + NAAT.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Which sputum pathogens are typically associated with bronchiectasis/cystic fibrosis versus alcoholics with cavitating pneumonia?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Bronchiectasis/CF: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Alcoholics / cavitating upper-lobe pneumonia: Klebsiella pneumoniae ('redcurrant jelly' sputum).

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: How should sputum be collected and processed when TB is suspected?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Send at least three deep-cough specimens (ideally including an early-morning sample). Each undergoes AFB smear (Ziehl-Neelsen/auramine), mycobacterial culture (gold standard, slow — weeks) and NAAT/GeneXpert (rapid, detects rifampicin resistance). Use induced sputum or BAL if unable to expectorate.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: What immediate infection-control steps are needed for a patient with suspected pulmonary TB?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Airborne (respiratory) isolation in a negative-pressure side room before results return, staff FFP3 masks, and notification to the local health protection team (TB is a notifiable disease). Do not delay these pending confirmation.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: What is the commonest bacterial cause of infectious diarrhoea in the UK, identified on stool culture?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Campylobacter (typically C. jejuni). Often causes bloody diarrhoea and abdominal pain; usually self-limiting, with clarithromycin/azithromycin reserved for severe or immunocompromised cases.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: How is Clostridioides difficile diagnosed on stool testing, and why can routine culture miss it?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: C. diff is a SEPARATE test that must be specifically requested. A two-step approach is used: GDH antigen screen plus toxin detection (or toxin PCR followed by toxin EIA). Standard bacterial culture will not report it unless asked.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Why must antibiotics and antimotility agents be AVOIDED in E. coli O157 (STEC/VTEC) infection?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: O157 produces Shiga toxin. Antibiotics and antimotility agents (e.g. loperamide) may increase toxin release/exposure and raise the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS), particularly in children. Management is supportive with monitoring for HUS.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: What is the classic triad of haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury (AKI). Most commonly follows E. coli O157 infection in children after an episode of bloody diarrhoea.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: When investigating for parasites (ova, cysts and parasites / OC&P), how many samples should be sent and why?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Send 3 separate stool samples because parasite shedding (e.g. Giardia, Entamoeba, Cryptosporidium) is intermittent, so a single sample may be falsely negative. Request specifically in prolonged or travel-associated diarrhoea.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: What organism does a throat swab primarily aim to detect, and why does it matter?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes, GAS) — the main treatable bacterial cause of pharyngitis/tonsillitis and the organism behind complications like scarlet fever, quinsy, rheumatic fever and post-strep glomerulonephritis.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Name the four Centor criteria.
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, history of fever, and absence of cough. Each scores 1 point; higher scores raise the probability of streptococcal infection and support considering antibiotics.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Why can a positive throat swab be misleading?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: It confirms the presence of GAS but cannot distinguish active infection from asymptomatic carriage, which is common (especially in children). Results must be interpreted with the clinical picture. Culture also has a 1–2 day delay.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Which antibiotic is first-line for confirmed/likely streptococcal sore throat, and which must be avoided?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) for 5–10 days is first-line. Avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin if glandular fever (EBV) is possible, as it causes a widespread maculopapular rash.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Which throat infections need special media or advance notice to the microbiology lab?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae — charcoal/tellurite medium; grey pseudomembrane; unvaccinated/travellers) and gonococcal pharyngitis (specific media or NAAT). Routine culture will miss both, so the lab must be informed.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Which GAS-related conditions are notifiable in the UK?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Scarlet fever and diphtheria are notifiable to Public Health. Scarlet fever presents with a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue following a GAS infection.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Does a positive wound swab confirm wound infection?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: No. All open wounds and chronic ulcers are colonised with bacteria, so a positive swab alone does not mean infection. Infection is a CLINICAL diagnosis (spreading erythema, warmth, increasing pain, purulence, systemic upset). Treat the patient, not the swab.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: When should you NOT take a wound swab?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: In a clinically uninfected wound or chronic ulcer (clean, granulating, no erythema/pain/purulence/systemic signs). Swabbing only grows colonisers and encourages inappropriate antibiotic use.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: How do you take a good-quality wound swab?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Cleanse/debride the wound first, then swab the deep advancing edge using a rotating (Levine) technique over healthy tissue, or express and send pus/tissue. Tissue biopsy or aspirated pus is superior to a superficial surface swab, which mostly grows skin flora.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Name common wound pathogens and their typical settings.
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Staph aureus incl. MRSA (commonest, SSIs); beta-haemolytic strep / Strep pyogenes (cellulitis, necrotising infection); Pseudomonas aeruginosa (moist wounds/burns, green discharge); anaerobes and mixed/polymicrobial flora (diabetic foot, pressure ulcers, bites).

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Which wound features signal necrotising fasciitis?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Pain out of proportion to appearance, rapidly spreading erythema/dusky skin, systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, hypotension) and crepitus. It is a surgical emergency — resuscitate, give broad-spectrum antibiotics and arrange urgent surgical debridement; do not wait for swab results.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: What organism is "Group B Streptococcus" and where does it colonise?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Streptococcus agalactiae — a Gram-positive coccus that is a common asymptomatic coloniser of the maternal vagina and rectum (recto-vaginal carriage). It is the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: Describe the GBS swab and what it detects.
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: A combined low vaginal + rectal (recto-vaginal) swab, ideally cultured on enriched (selective) media to maximise sensitivity. It detects transient, asymptomatic carriage (colonisation) — it is NOT a test of infection.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: How does the UK approach GBS prevention, and what is the key intervention?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: Risk-factor-based (RCOG), NOT universal antenatal screening. The intervention is intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP): IV benzylpenicillin during labour, or clindamycin if penicillin-allergic. Antenatal treatment of carriage is not used as it does not prevent recolonisation by delivery.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: List the main indications for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) for GBS.
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: GBS detected in current pregnancy (incidental swab or GBS bacteriuria), a previous baby with GBS disease, preterm labour, prolonged rupture of membranes, and intrapartum fever / suspected chorioamnionitis.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.front: How does early-onset neonatal GBS disease present, and how is a septic-appearing neonate managed?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.back: First week of life: respiratory distress, temperature instability, poor feeding/lethargy; can progress rapidly to sepsis and meningitis. Manage a septic-appearing neonate as early-onset GBS until proven otherwise — take cultures and start empirical IV antibiotics immediately.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.front: What colour are Gram-positive vs Gram-negative organisms, and why?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.back: Gram-positive = purple/blue (thick peptidoglycan retains the crystal violet–iodine complex during decolourisation). Gram-negative = pink/red (thin wall + outer membrane loses crystal violet and takes up the safranin counterstain).

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.front: Gram-positive cocci: how do you distinguish Staphylococcus from Streptococcus?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.back: Arrangement + catalase. Clusters = Staphylococcus (catalase positive). Chains or pairs = Streptococcus/Enterococcus (catalase negative). Lancet-shaped diplococci = Strep pneumoniae.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.front: A CSF Gram stain shows Gram-negative diplococci. Likely organism and immediate action?
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.back: Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus). Give empirical antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone) immediately — do not wait for the Gram stain or culture.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.front: Name organisms that Gram stain poorly or not at all, and the alternative approach.
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.back: Mycobacteria (use Ziehl-Neelsen/auramine — acid-fast), Mycoplasma (no cell wall), Treponema/spirochaetes (dark-field/serology), Legionella and Chlamydia (culture/PCR/antigen).

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.front: Gram-positive bacilli (rods) — name the classic genera.
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.back: Clostridium, Listeria, Bacillus and Corynebacterium. Listeria is a key cause of meningitis in neonates, the elderly and the immunosuppressed.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 68-year-old man with a central venous catheter has one of two blood culture sets grow coagulase-negative staphylococci after 3 days (long time-to-positivity). He is clinically well and afebrile. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Definite catheter-related bloodstream infection requiring immediate line removal
Likely skin contaminant given single positive set and long time-to-positivity
Candidaemia requiring ophthalmology review
Staph aureus bacteraemia requiring echocardiography
Confirmed infective endocarditis
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Likely skin contaminant given single positive set and long time-to-positivity
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Coagulase-negative staphylococci growing in only 1 of 2 sets with a long time-to-positivity, in a well patient, is the classic picture of a skin contaminant rather than a true pathogen. True infection is more likely when both sets grow the same organism with short time-to-positivity.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A septic patient's blood cultures grow Staph aureus in both sets. Which of the following is the most important next step?
options: Repeat cultures only if the patient deteriorates
Treat with a short oral course and discharge
Search for endocarditis/deep focus, remove lines, and repeat cultures to confirm clearance
Dismiss it as a probable skin contaminant
Stop antibiotics as one positive set is insufficient
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Search for endocarditis/deep focus, remove lines, and repeat cultures to confirm clearance
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Staph aureus bacteraemia is never ignored: it mandates a search for a deep focus or endocarditis (echocardiography), removal of any lines, and repeat cultures to document clearance. Staph aureus is almost never a contaminant.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: When taking blood cultures in a patient with suspected sepsis, which single factor most improves the diagnostic yield?
options: Drawing the sample from an existing indwelling cannula
Taking an adequate blood volume (~8–10 mL per bottle)
Warming the bottles before inoculation
Using a smaller-gauge needle
Filling only the anaerobic bottle
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Taking an adequate blood volume (~8–10 mL per bottle)
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Blood volume is the main determinant of yield — under-filling causes false negatives. Drawing from an existing line risks contamination and is reserved for investigating line infection. Both aerobic and anaerobic bottles should be filled.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 24-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant is asymptomatic. A routine antenatal MSU grows >10^5 CFU/mL of E. coli sensitive to nitrofurantoin. What is the most appropriate management?
options: No antibiotics as she is asymptomatic
Repeat the MSU in 4 weeks and treat only if still positive
Treat with an appropriate antibiotic now
Reassure and treat only if she develops dysuria
Send early-morning urines for AFB
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Treat with an appropriate antibiotic now
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is normally not treated, but pregnancy is a key exception: untreated bacteriuria increases the risk of pyelonephritis and preterm birth, so it should be treated with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic guided by sensitivities.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 30-year-old man has persistent dysuria and frequency. Urine microscopy shows marked pyuria but routine culture is repeatedly negative. Which investigation is most important to exclude a specific, treatable cause?
options: Cystoscopy
Early-morning urines for acid-fast bacilli
Serum PSA
24-hour urinary protein
Renal ultrasound only
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Early-morning urines for acid-fast bacilli
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Sterile pyuria (pyuria with negative routine culture) should prompt consideration of renal tract TB. Three early-morning urine specimens for AFB microscopy and mycobacterial culture are the classic investigation; chlamydia/urethritis is also a common cause.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: An 82-year-old nursing-home resident with stable chronic confusion and no fever, dysuria or new symptoms has a dipstick positive for nitrites and leucocytes; MSU grows E. coli. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Start empirical oral antibiotics for the positive dipstick
Start IV antibiotics for presumed urosepsis
Do not start antibiotics; look for another cause of any concern
Insert a urinary catheter to obtain a clean sample
Treat only if repeat culture is positive
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Do not start antibiotics; look for another cause of any concern
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is very common in elderly and institutionalised patients and should not be treated in the absence of specific UTI symptoms or systemic sepsis. Dipsticks are unreliable in this group; antibiotics drive resistance without benefit.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 68-year-old man with COPD produces a sputum sample. The laboratory Gram film report reads: 'Numerous squamous epithelial cells, scanty neutrophils, mixed oral flora.' What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The sample is a good lower-respiratory specimen and culture results can be relied upon
The sample is contaminated with saliva/upper-airway flora and is of poor diagnostic quality
This confirms a polymicrobial pneumonia requiring broad-spectrum antibiotics
This is diagnostic of aspiration pneumonia
The epithelial cells indicate active alveolar infection
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: The sample is contaminated with saliva/upper-airway flora and is of poor diagnostic quality
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Many squamous epithelial cells with few neutrophils indicates the specimen is largely saliva/upper-airway secretions, not lower-respiratory purulent sputum. Culture from such a sample is unreliable and a repeat deep-cough specimen should be requested. Abundant neutrophils with few epithelial cells would indicate a good sample.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 55-year-old presents with severe community-acquired pneumonia (CURB-65 = 4). Routine sputum and blood cultures are sent and are negative at 48 hours, yet he remains febrile and hypoxic. Which investigation is most likely to establish the microbiological diagnosis?
options: Repeat routine sputum culture on standard blood agar
Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigen tests
Waiting a further 72 hours for the original culture to grow
Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear
Aspergillus galactomannan
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigen tests
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Atypical organisms such as Legionella do not grow on routine culture, so negative routine cultures do not exclude them. Urinary antigen testing (Legionella and pneumococcus) provides a rapid diagnosis in severe CAP; Mycoplasma/Chlamydophila serology or PCR are alternatives. Empirical cover should already include a macrolide.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 34-year-old man with 6 weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss has a cavitating right-upper-lobe lesion on chest X-ray. Which single test on his sputum most rapidly identifies Mycobacterium tuberculosis AND detects rifampicin resistance?
options: Ziehl-Neelsen (AFB) smear
Solid Lowenstein-Jensen mycobacterial culture
Nucleic acid amplification test (GeneXpert MTB/RIF)
Routine bacterial culture and sensitivity
Tuberculin skin (Mantoux) test
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Nucleic acid amplification test (GeneXpert MTB/RIF)
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: NAAT/GeneXpert gives a result within hours, confirms M. tuberculosis and simultaneously detects rifampicin resistance, guiding early therapy and isolation decisions. AFB smear is rapid but non-specific and less sensitive; mycobacterial culture is the gold standard for full sensitivities but takes weeks; Mantoux indicates exposure, not active disease.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 4-year-old girl presents with 3 days of bloody diarrhoea and abdominal pain after a farm visit. She is now pale and lethargic with reduced urine output. Bloods show Hb 78 g/L, platelets 45 x10^9/L, and creatinine markedly raised for age. A blood film shows fragmented red cells. Which organism is most likely responsible, and what is the key management principle?
options: Campylobacter jejuni — start clarithromycin promptly
E. coli O157 (STEC) — supportive care, AVOID antibiotics and antimotility agents
Shigella dysenteriae — start ciprofloxacin
Salmonella enteritidis — start intravenous ceftriaxone
Clostridioides difficile — start oral vancomycin
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: E. coli O157 (STEC) — supportive care, AVOID antibiotics and antimotility agents
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: The picture is haemolytic uraemic syndrome (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, AKI) following bloody diarrhoea, classically due to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157 after farm/animal contact. Management is supportive with monitoring of renal function; antibiotics and antimotility agents are avoided as they may increase toxin release and the risk of HUS.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 72-year-old man develops profuse watery diarrhoea 6 days into a course of co-amoxiclav for a chest infection. He is febrile with a raised white cell count and abdominal tenderness. Which single stool investigation is most appropriate to confirm the likely diagnosis?
options: Routine bacterial culture for Salmonella and Campylobacter
Microscopy for ova, cysts and parasites
C. difficile GDH antigen plus toxin testing
Faecal calprotectin
Stool viral PCR for norovirus
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: C. difficile GDH antigen plus toxin testing
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea with systemic features strongly suggests C. difficile infection. This requires a specifically requested test — a two-step GDH antigen plus toxin assay (or toxin PCR then toxin EIA) — as routine bacterial culture and OC&P will not detect it. Management includes stopping the offending antibiotic, oral vancomycin first-line, isolation, and avoiding antimotility agents.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 25-year-old man returns from a 3-week trip to India with 4 weeks of intermittent bloating, foul-smelling loose stools and flatulence. He is systemically well and afebrile. A single stool culture is negative. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Repeat routine bacterial culture once
Send 3 separate stool samples for microscopy (ova, cysts and parasites)
Request C. difficile toxin testing
Faecal calprotectin and urgent colonoscopy
Blood cultures for enteric fever
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Send 3 separate stool samples for microscopy (ova, cysts and parasites)
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Prolonged, non-bloody, travel-associated diarrhoea with bloating and flatulence is characteristic of giardiasis. Parasite shedding is intermittent, so 3 separate samples should be sent for OC&P microscopy to improve sensitivity. C. diff is not suggested (no antibiotic exposure), and he is systemically well making enteric fever less likely as the immediate priority.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 7-year-old presents with a 2-day sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes but no cough. His parents ask for antibiotics. What is the most appropriate initial approach in UK practice?
options: Send a throat swab and withhold all treatment until culture returns
Prescribe amoxicillin immediately
Use a clinical score (Centor/FeverPAIN); with a high score, consider phenoxymethylpenicillin
Prescribe a macrolide as first-line for everyone with a sore throat
Reassure and discharge with no assessment as all sore throats are viral
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Use a clinical score (Centor/FeverPAIN); with a high score, consider phenoxymethylpenicillin
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: NICE recommends using Centor or FeverPAIN to guide antibiotic decisions rather than routinely swabbing. This child scores highly (exudate, nodes, fever, no cough = Centor 4), so phenoxymethylpenicillin is appropriate. Amoxicillin is avoided because of the EBV rash risk; macrolides are reserved for penicillin allergy.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 19-year-old with a severe sore throat, marked cervical lymphadenopathy and lethargy is given amoxicillin and develops a widespread maculopapular rash. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: True penicillin (IgE-mediated) allergy
Infectious mononucleosis (EBV)
Scarlet fever
Diphtheria
Gonococcal pharyngitis
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV)
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: A maculopapular rash after amoxicillin/ampicillin in a young person with pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy is classic for glandular fever (EBV). It is not a true penicillin allergy. This is why phenoxymethylpenicillin, not amoxicillin, is preferred when EBV is possible; confirm with Monospot/atypical lymphocytes.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: An unvaccinated traveller returns with a sore throat and a firm, adherent grey membrane over the tonsils and pharynx. What is the most important action regarding the throat swab?
options: Send a routine throat swab; no special handling is required
Inform the laboratory of suspected diphtheria so appropriate selective media are used
Rely on a rapid strep antigen test alone to confirm the diagnosis
Send the swab for EBV serology
Delay swabbing until antibiotics have been started
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Inform the laboratory of suspected diphtheria so appropriate selective media are used
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: A grey pseudomembrane in an unvaccinated traveller suggests diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae), which requires special charcoal/tellurite selective media — routine culture will miss it, so the lab must be told. Diphtheria is a notifiable, potentially airway-threatening emergency and does not present as EBV or GAS on rapid antigen testing.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 68-year-old man with a chronic venous leg ulcer attends for a routine dressing change. The ulcer is granulating, non-tender, with no surrounding erythema, warmth or discharge. He is systemically well and afebrile. A wound swab taken at a previous visit grew Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Prescribe a 7-day course of oral flucloxacillin
Continue standard wound care and dressings without antibiotics
Refer urgently for surgical debridement
Start oral ciprofloxacin to cover Pseudomonas
Apply a topical antibiotic to the ulcer bed
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Continue standard wound care and dressings without antibiotics
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: The ulcer is colonised, not infected — there are no clinical signs of infection. A positive swab in a clinically uninfected ulcer reflects colonisation and should not be treated. Antibiotics are only indicated when there are clinical signs of infection. Treat the patient, not the swab.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with a 6-hour history of severe pain in his lower leg. The pain is far greater than the modest overlying erythema would suggest. Over the past 2 hours the redness has spread visibly, the skin is becoming dusky, and there is crepitus on palpation. He is febrile (39.1C), tachycardic and hypotensive. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Take a superficial wound swab and await sensitivities before treating
Prescribe oral flucloxacillin and review in 48 hours
Resuscitate, give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and call surgery for urgent debridement
Elevate the limb and apply a compression bandage
Arrange an outpatient MRI to confirm the diagnosis
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Resuscitate, give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and call surgery for urgent debridement
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: Pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading dusky erythema, crepitus and systemic toxicity indicate necrotising fasciitis — a surgical emergency. Management is aggressive resuscitation, urgent broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and immediate surgical debridement. Do not delay for swab results or imaging; delay increases mortality.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 40-year-old woman has a clinically infected surgical wound with spreading erythema and purulent discharge. The team wants a wound sample to guide antibiotic therapy. Which sampling approach gives the most reliable microbiological result?
options: A quick swab of the dry, intact skin adjacent to the wound
Swabbing the surface slough without cleansing the wound first
Cleansing/debriding first, then sampling deep tissue or aspirated pus from the advancing edge
Sending the removed dressing to the laboratory
Swabbing only after a full course of empirical antibiotics has finished
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Cleansing/debriding first, then sampling deep tissue or aspirated pus from the advancing edge
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: A superficial swab mostly grows surface colonisers and skin flora. Cleansing/debriding first and then sampling deep tissue or aspirated pus from the advancing edge (e.g. Levine technique) gives results most representative of the true pathogen. Tissue biopsy or aspirated pus is superior to a dry surface swab, and samples should ideally be taken before antibiotics.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 29-year-old woman at 36 weeks' gestation has an incidental positive low vaginal-rectal swab for Group B Streptococcus after a swab taken for another reason. She is well and asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management regarding GBS?
options: Start oral amoxicillin now for 7 days to eradicate carriage before delivery
Offer intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin during labour
Arrange elective caesarean section to avoid vertical transmission
Repeat the swab weekly and treat only if it remains positive at term
No action is needed as GBS carriage is harmless
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Offer intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin during labour
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: GBS detected in the current pregnancy is an indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) with IV benzylpenicillin, given during labour to reduce vertical transmission and early-onset neonatal disease. Antenatal antibiotics do not prevent recolonisation by delivery, so they are not used to 'eradicate' carriage. Caesarean is not indicated purely for GBS colonisation, and the UK does not use a repeat-screen-and-treat-antenatally strategy.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A 32-year-old woman is in established labour at 39 weeks. She reports a genuine anaphylactic allergy to penicillin. Her notes show GBS bacteriuria was treated earlier in this pregnancy. Which intrapartum antibiotic is most appropriate for GBS prophylaxis?
options: IV benzylpenicillin
IV clindamycin
IV gentamicin
Oral erythromycin
No prophylaxis is required as the bacteriuria was already treated
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: IV clindamycin
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: GBS bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated at the time and also flags the need for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. The first-line IAP agent is IV benzylpenicillin, but in a penicillin-allergic woman (particularly with anaphylaxis) IV clindamycin is the appropriate alternative. Earlier treatment of the bacteriuria does not remove the need for intrapartum prophylaxis.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.question: A term baby is 18 hours old. The mother had GBS detected this pregnancy but delivered precipitously before IV antibiotics could be given. The baby now has grunting, tachypnoea, temperature instability and is feeding poorly. What is the single most important immediate action?
options: Take blood cultures and start empirical IV antibiotics without delay
Send a superficial ear and skin swab and await results before treating
Reassure and observe for a further 12 hours as symptoms are often benign
Start oral antibiotics and discharge with community midwife follow-up
Perform an urgent lumbar puncture before giving any antibiotics
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.answer: Take blood cultures and start empirical IV antibiotics without delay
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures &.explanation: This is early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis until proven otherwise: respiratory distress, temperature instability and poor feeding in the first week, with maternal GBS and no intrapartum prophylaxis. It can progress rapidly to septic shock and meningitis. The priority is to take cultures and start empirical IV antibiotics immediately; investigations such as lumbar puncture should not delay antibiotics, and observation alone or oral antibiotics with discharge would be dangerous.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.question: A 19-year-old presents with fever, neck stiffness and a non-blanching purpuric rash. A CSF Gram stain shows Gram-negative diplococci. Which is the most likely causative organism?
options: Streptococcus pneumoniae
Neisseria meningitidis
Listeria monocytogenes
Haemophilus influenzae
Staphylococcus aureus
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.explanation: Gram-negative diplococci in CSF with a purpuric rash in a young adult is classic meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis). Pneumococcus is Gram-positive diplococci; Listeria is Gram-positive bacilli. Antibiotics must be given immediately without waiting for confirmation.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.question: A wound swab grows Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive. Which organism is most consistent with these findings?
options: Streptococcus pyogenes
Enterococcus faecalis
Staphylococcus aureus
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Escherichia coli
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.explanation: Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive indicate Staphylococcus (S. aureus). Streptococci and enterococci form chains/pairs and are catalase negative. Neisseria is Gram-negative diplococci and E. coli is a Gram-negative bacillus.

investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.question: A patient with cough, weight loss and haemoptysis has sputum that fails to Gram stain despite clear infection. Which stain is most appropriate to identify the likely organism?
options: Repeat Gram stain with fresh reagents
Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain
India ink stain
Silver stain
Giemsa stain
investigations__MICROBIOLOGY__Stains & M.explanation: The picture suggests tuberculosis. Mycobacteria have a waxy, mycolic-acid-rich wall that resists Gram staining, so a Ziehl-Neelsen (or auramine) acid-fast stain is used. India ink is for Cryptococcus and silver stains for fungi/Pneumocystis.
